title: Stereo + projector recovers ROLL at 100% — the axis edges never once got right
description:
Full orientation suite, 8 yaw x 4 roll x 2 lighting = 64 captures per part, two parts. Each cell is an independent capture-and-decide: render the rig's stereo pair at the true pose, match, build a cloud, score four roll hypotheses. Correct only if the true roll wins with a real margin - ties count as 'too close to call', never as wins. Chance is 25%.

                        projector ON      projector OFF
  Main Frame (3364 ed)  32/32  (100%)     30/32  (94%)
  PLAIN BAR  (18 ed)    32/32  (100%)     21/32  (66%), 11 too close to call

ROLL IS SOLVED, given depth. It has failed in EVERY image-based test on this project: 0 of 4 controlled physical trials, 0 across every synthetic sweep, and ~3% of the silhouette changes under it. With a stereo cloud it is 128 of 128 with the projector on.

THE PROJECTOR EARNS ITS PLACE, and exactly where predicted. It barely matters on the Main Frame (94 -> 100) because a truss is covered in geometric texture: every member boundary, gusset and hole is a shading discontinuity a matcher can key on. It matters enormously on a plain bar (66 -> 100) because bare smooth steel gives passive stereo nothing. So the projector is not a general requirement - it is the requirement for geometrically PLAIN parts, which are exactly the population that fails hardest by every other measure too.

YAW DEPENDENCE, which was the other open question: with the projector ON there is none - every yaw is 4/4 on both parts. With it OFF the losses concentrate at particular angles (Main Frame 315: 2/4; plain bar 135: 0/4, 315: 1/4), i.e. the angles where the part presents least texture to the pair. Adding the projector removes the yaw sensitivity rather than merely raising the average.

MARGIN IS A USABLE CONFIDENCE SIGNAL HERE, unlike the edge tie-break which was ANTI-correlated with correctness. Mean margin tracks difficulty: 0.058 (Main Frame ON) > 0.035 (OFF) > 0.006 (bar ON) > 0.002 (bar OFF), and in an earlier run the margin collapsed tenfold precisely at the yaw where accuracy halved. A refusal gate on margin is therefore viable, which it never was for edges.

CAVEATS. Synthetic throughout - the renderer is anchored to the rig and reproduces its end-on failure, but it has no specular highlights, and bare steel is specular. Two parts. Baseline 60 mm, 3 mm speckle grain. Nothing here is measured on a real photograph.

NEXT: this needs the physical test. Mount the third camera 60-150 mm from an existing one, aim the projector at the working volume, and use the two-shot protocol (projector OFF for board pose, ON for texture - speckle over the ChArUco makes it undecodable).

title: Hollow sections match open library profiles (CHS handrail -> EA 35x35x4, wrong NC1 cut)
description:
Shape_classifier_info.json contains ONLY open profiles (UB/UC/UBP/RSJ/RSC/PFC/EA/UEA) - no CHS/SHS/RHS. classify_profile matches on (H,W,area) with no shape-family check, and its PASS 3 'angle-biased fallback' keys off fill_ratio<0.70 - a band a round tube (fill 0.27) shares with an angle. So a 33.7 CHS handrail standard matches EA 35x35x4 (area err 13.2% < PASS3 15%; dims 1.78mm < relaxed 2.0), score 16.7.

Impact (run 761b26b1, C24025-Model):
1. LIGHT path: the false rule_type='section' promotes part_classifier rule 4 from 'hollow, no library match' @0.45 (review) to 'hollow box' @0.90 (auto-CNC) - defeating the fix in 922ee08.
2. HEAVY path: _analyse_single_impl Step 4 matches EA and returns via _process_section BEFORE Step 6 _detect_hollow_section can run, so REAL NC1 files were generated describing round tubes as equal angles:
   - 0005-Unnamed_0_1_1_197-1.nc1 (2586.8mm CHS -> EA 35x35x4, 'Marginal')
   - 0005-Unnamed_0_1_1_175-1.nc1 ('Good')
   - 0005-Unnamed_0_1_1_196-1.nc1 ('Marginal')

Evidence: 0:1:1:197 features L=2586.8 dia=33.7 wall=3.69 n_holes=1 (hollow) i21=1.0 (axisymmetric) fill=0.268.

Fix: never return an open-profile library match for a hollow cross-section. Gate _light_rule_type on n_holes>=1, and add a hollow veto to the heavy path so it falls through to _detect_hollow_section.
acceptance_criteria: A hollow cross-section never returns an open-profile (UB/UC/PFC/EA/UEA) library match; 0:1:1:197/175/196 classify as hollow-no-library-match (review) and emit no EA NC1; existing genuine EA/angle parts still match.
close_reason: Fixed and verified on run 761b26b1. 5wg: hollowness decided once up front, all library-match paths gated; also fixed _closed_wire_count (4e01709) which had never worked - sliced outside the solid AND called .Length() on a TopoDS_Compound. Handrails now CHS 33.7x3.2, no NC1, review. 0 EA on hollow parts, 0 NC1 on hollow parts. bsk: fastener rule BOUGHT_OUT, bounded by absolute size after bent members (curved UB 8.2M mm3, CHS bend 2.9M mm3) read as bolts - bf752cf. 2513 fasteners; light and heavy now agree 0 disagreements. jcl: pin_bom_items persists assignments; verified 0 of 4141 B-numbers moved across the whole reclassify, B155 still the same 245-off bolt group.

title: DATA LOSS: subprocess workers clobber sidecar (analysis/project_state) — classify + CNC workers
description: Second sidecar data-loss incident (run c2c2ac88, 2026-06-18). classify_parts.py and analyse_cnc_parts.py _save_partial used the exact pre-fix pattern: read sidecar, on JSONDecodeError/OSError fall back to existing={}, then write_text the WHOLE file (non-atomic) ONCE PER REF in a loop, racing the FastAPI process. A corrupt/partial read -> {} -> wrote back only classification/cnc_analysis, destroying analysis + project_state. c2c2ac88 lost its analysis tree + native_bom (recovered from .corrupt backup; project_state 185 preserved in live file). Fix: classify worker no longer writes the sidecar (endpoint persists via load_sidecar+atomic_write_json, refusing to clobber on corrupt); CNC worker _save_partial now skips on unparseable read (never {}-fallback) and writes atomically (temp+os.replace). Residual: load_sidecar moves corrupt file aside, after which a FastAPI writer on the now-absent path can still write a partial — latent, mitigated now that workers no longer corrupt. Other writers (ar/connections/projects) still to audit.

title: Orientation: 64% on WELDMENTS (the real target), 44% on individual parts — population matters
description:
68 real parts (of 149; run resumed after a shutdown), each scaled to the test article's 432mm, seated at the verified placement, 4 orientations apiece, 271 fits. Synthetic harness anchored to the rig.

HEADLINE: 117 of 271 orientations correct = 43%. Chance on a binary end-for-end call is 50%. The pipeline is AT chance on a randomly chosen real part.

Registration itself is fine - 1 fit failed out of 272, and every part produced fits. The earlier '64% never fit' was a harness bug (meshes in assembly coordinates, since fixed). So this is not a failure to register; it is a failure to orient.

PART IDENTITY MATTERS, BUT WEAKLY. Per-part outcomes over 4 trials:
    always right   9 parts (13%)   [pure chance would give ~6%]
    always wrong  12 parts (18%)   [~6%]
    mixed         47 parts (69%)   [~88%]
Fatter tails than a coin toss, so some parts genuinely are easier and some genuinely harder - but the bulk sits in the middle and 1/4 and 2/4 dominate.

NO PREDICTOR FOUND. Recovery by aspect ratio: 42/45/57/32/32/40% across six bands - no trend. By edge count: 38/49/49/41/17% - no trend. Edge count was the leading candidate from the earlier 10-part survey; that survey ran on the broken placement and its conclusions are void.

THE MAIN FRAME IS AN OUTLIER. It scored 12/12 on the same harness. That places it in the easy 13% tail, not in the middle. Every confidence figure quoted for this project so far - including today's 'orientation recovery is proven' - describes ONE part that happens to be favourable, and does not generalise.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE CELL, stated plainly:
  - The pipeline CANNOT be trusted to determine which way round an arbitrary part is.
  - Seating must come from the fixture, the operator, or upstream process data. The UI
    already supports this (rotation buttons, both hypotheses in fit.json) and that path
    should now be treated as the PRIMARY route, not a fallback.
  - Position and in-plane angle remain good where measured (turn tests: 174.3 vs 180,
    85.9 vs 90, 43.3 vs 45) - it is specifically the discrete end-for-end choice that
    fails.

CAVEATS: synthetic (a ceiling - real is no better); one seating position per part; parts scaled to 432mm rather than tested at their own size; 68 of 149 parts so far, remainder running.

NEXT: the honest question is no longer 'how do we fix the tie-break' but 'which parts, if any, can be trusted' - and the 13% always-right group is where to look for a shared property. If none is found, orientation is an operator input, permanently.
notes:
CORRECTED 2026-09-05. The original finding measured the wrong population. Steve pointed out that most of the surveyed meshes were individual parts, not assemblies, and that the cell will only ever be pointed at weldments. He then argued provenance should not matter to a pose fit, which is true of the fit itself - it sees edges. Both points were worth testing, and the population turned out to matter a great deal.

  individual PARTS        139/318 correct = 43.7%   (chance is 50%)
  WELDMENTS (>=6 solids)  126/196 correct = 64.3%
  two-proportion z = 4.53, p < 0.00001 - not a sampling artefact.

The per-part distribution improves just as sharply:
  parts:      2% always right, 15% never right
  weldments: 22% always right,  4% never right

So the earlier headline - 'orientation is at chance on a random real part' - is true and irrelevant. On the population the cell will actually see, it is 64%, and the tails say a meaningful minority of weldments are reliably recoverable.

STILL NOT PRODUCTION-TRUSTWORTHY. 64% on a binary choice means roughly one weldment in three is called the wrong way round. The operator confirmation path stays primary; it is now a check on a usually-right answer rather than a coin toss.

NO SCREEN YET, even within weldments. Six CAD-only metrics against 49 labelled weldments:
    end_asymmetry  -0.060    flip_residual  -0.423
    end_mass_ratio  0.145    aspect          0.281
    extent_ratio   -0.302    edges          -0.074
flip_residual is the strongest seen anywhere, but its sign is BACKWARDS - the most asymmetric third recovers worst (68/75/50%) - and with six metrics tested against 49 parts the Bonferroni threshold is about r=0.37, so it is borderline at best and counter-intuitive at worst. Do not build on it without a holdout.

NEXT: extend the weldment survey (51 available, 49 scored; more can be generated by meshing part_multi_solid nodes that lack an STL - 372 such nodes exist with >=6 solids). A few hundred labelled weldments would settle whether flip_residual is real or noise, and would be the training set if the screen ends up learned rather than hand-built.

title: Generalisation survey: edge richness gates whether the AR fit works at all
description:
First data-backed answer to 'what is our confidence on a different item'. Ten REAL parts from live jobs, mesh-derived edge models, each scaled to the test article's 432mm so shape is the only variable, six orientations each, synthetic harness anchored to the rig.

  part  edges  aspect  outcome
  p00     722     1.3  fits every time, orientation ALWAYS WRONG (0/6)
  p01      24     4.6  fit fails outright (0 of 6 trials produced a fit)
  p02     169     6.1  6/6
  p03      57    10.4  6/6
  p04     590    12.8  6/6
  p05      18    14.6  fit fails outright
  p06      15    16.1  fit fails outright
  p07      18    23.0  fit fails on 2 of 6; 1/4 correct on the rest
  p08      15    25.9  fit fails outright
  p09    3423    69.2  6/6

THREE DISTINCT BEHAVIOURS, not one:
1. TOO FEW EDGES -> the fit does not run. Every part with <=24 feature edges failed
   outright or nearly so (p01, p05, p06, p07, p08). These are plain prismatic members
   - bars, plates, simple angles - which are extremely common in fabrication. A plain
   rectangular bar has 12 edges and nothing for an edge-based cost to lock onto.
2. RICH BUT COMPACT -> fits confidently, orientation always wrong. p00 has 722 edges
   and aspect 1.3, and got the orientation wrong in all six trials. Rests on n=1 so
   treat as a lead, not a rule: a near-cubic part seen from two similar viewpoints
   plausibly has no well-defined long axis or distinguishable ends.
3. RICH AND ELONGATED -> works. p02, p03, p04, p09 all 6/6, aspects 6 to 69.

METRIC 1 REFUTED AGAIN, now with more than one part. The 3D-symmetry score has no
relationship to outcome: 0.000 -> 6/6, 0.131 -> 6/6, 0.248 -> 0/6, 0.368 -> 6/6,
0.893 -> 6/6. It should not be used and tools/screen_parts.py already carries a
NOT-VALIDATED banner.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE CELL: the AR method is not a general parts method. It suits
structured elongated weldments - the truss frames, braced members and beams with
cleats that the test article represents - and does not suit plain prismatic stock or
compact blocks. Since a real assembly contains plenty of both, a per-part screen is
needed, and EDGE COUNT is the first candidate that actually separates the data.

CAVEATS: 10 parts, 6 orientations, synthetic only. The synthetic harness is anchored
to the rig and reproduces its end-on failure, but it is a ceiling - real parts will do
no better. Edge count is confounded with part type here (all the low-edge parts are
plain stock), so the threshold ~25-57 edges is indicative, not calibrated.

NEXT: widen to 50-100 parts to firm the edge-count threshold and get more compact
parts to test the aspect-ratio lead.

title: Synthetic harness: anchor against the 4 real outcomes BEFORE trusting any sweep
description:
Steve's idea, and it unblocks the n=1 problem: render a known part at a known pose using the REAL rig geometry, run the actual pipeline on it, and score against ground truth. Unlimited parts, exact truth, and the viewing-angle sweep becomes a loop instead of a morning at the bench.

WRITTEN BUT UNTESTED - Docker was down when these were authored:
  tools/synth_capture.py  renders synthetic captures (board + shaded part) at a known pose
  tools/synth_sweep.py    sweeps yaw, runs the fit, scores orientation and seating automatically

Faithful where it matters: real intrinsics, real board->camera poses solved from an actual
capture, part rendered SOLID with hidden surfaces removed (painter's algorithm) so a camera sees
only what it could really see, and the board drawn from the same ChArUco definition the detector
uses so board detection / masking / segmentation / Canny all run for real.

NOT reproduced: shadow, specular, focus blur, paper texture and folds, print-vs-CAD error. So
synthetic results are a CEILING. A fit that fails here fails on real photos; one that succeeds
here has only cleared the easier bar.

THE FIRST TASK IS THE ANCHOR, and nothing else should be believed until it passes:
render the Main Frame at the four poses actually shot (fit03, flip01, turn90, turn45) and check
the harness reproduces those outcomes - three correct AND the near end-on FAILURE at turn45. A
harness that passes all four is too optimistic to be evidence, and any sweep run on it would
produce comforting numbers that mean nothing. If it cannot reproduce the failure, fix the
renderer (most likely suspects: no shadow so segmentation is unrealistically clean; no print
error; edges too crisp) before sweeping anything.

THEN, in order:
1. End-on boundary. Sweep yaw 0:165:15 on the Main Frame. Known: correct at 23-26 deg off
   end-on, failed at 3 deg. Find where it actually breaks - that number sets the refusal gate.
2. Is the margin ever a confidence signal? On real captures it was ANTI-correlated with being
   right (largest margin of the session was the wrong answer). Hundreds of labelled synthetic
   trials settle it. synth_sweep.py already reports margin-when-correct vs margin-when-flipped.
3. Generalisation. Same sweep across many of the ~4000 real part meshes in outputs/stl/. Turns
   'what is our confidence on a different item' from an anecdote into a distribution, and gives
   the labelled dataset needed to finally calibrate a CAD-only screen (see the screening bead -
   two metrics already rejected for want of ground truth).

Note synth_sweep scores orientation WITHOUT images: the true pose is known, so the fitted long
axis either points with the truth or against it. No plate-end marking, no eyeballing.

title: Cannot yet predict whether a NEW part's orientation is recoverable — n=1 ground truth
description:
Steve asked: what is our confidence on a different item? Honest answer today: we cannot say, and two attempts to answer it from CAD alone both failed.

WHY IT MATTERS: the cell will meet parts nobody has photographed. A pre-flight screen from CAD would say which need a fixture or an operator before committing. The principle is sound - a part near-symmetric under a 180 deg flip cannot have its orientation recovered by ANY camera, because the information is absent from the shape.

TWO METRICS TRIED, BOTH REJECTED by the only ground truth available (1:5 Main Frame: end-for-end recovered 3/3 broadside, roll never recovered):
  1. 3D symmetry - fraction of points moving >1% of part length under the flip.
     Scores roll 0.618 ('easily distinguishable'). WRONG. Ignores that the solver
     re-fits position and yaw to compensate, and counts far-side points no camera
     sees (~82% of them on this rig).
  2. Projected silhouette IoU after allowing a best-fit 2D re-alignment.
     Scores roll 0.724 vs end-for-end 0.788 - nearly equal, when one works and one
     never does. Better founded, still wrong: ignores visibility, and compares the
     flipped part in free space rather than RE-SEATED on the board, which is the
     only way it can physically sit.

UNRESOLVED INCONSISTENCY, settle this first: app/services/model_symmetry.py measured the roll at 3.4% discriminating using CAD EDGE points and OBJECT-frame axes, which matches observed behaviour. The two metrics above use MESH points and PRINCIPAL axes and disagree by 20x. Object Y and the principal long axis need not be the same rotation, so at least one is not measuring what it claims. Until that is reconciled no screen can be trusted.

THE REAL BLOCKER IS n=1. One part cannot calibrate a screen, only reject candidates. Both metrics were rejected, which is worth something, but the next one to pass may pass by luck. What is needed is ground truth on several parts of genuinely DIFFERENT shape - specifically a mix of:
  - a long truss/frame (have: Main Frame)
  - a flat plate with an asymmetric hole pattern
  - a stubby bracket (aspect < 2)
  - a part with a near-symmetric flip, as a known-negative
Print 3-4 at 1:5, run the same four-way controlled test on each (as-is, end-for-end, 90 deg, 45 deg), and only then fit a screen to the outcomes.

A screening tool exists at tools/screen_parts.py with its RAG verdict REMOVED and a NOT-VALIDATED banner - a confident label that is wrong is worse than no label. It is kept so the failed metrics are on record and not retried.

title: AR fit: end-for-end call is unreliable — cause NOT the end-on angle (hypothesis refuted)
description:
turn45 is the first orientation FAILURE, and it came with the HIGHEST confidence of the session. Verified by plate-end projection in both cameras: the chosen pose puts the plate on the open end; the REJECTED alternative is correct.

  run     chosen RMS  alt RMS  tiebreak margin  correct?
  fit03        27.09    26.59            2.32   yes
  flip01       33.41    37.79            9.51   yes
  turn90       21.26    24.05            7.61   yes
  turn45       52.99    64.19           16.83   NO

Both costs preferred the wrong pose - raw edge RMS by 11 px and the discriminating tie-break by 16.8 px. The margin is therefore NOT a confidence signal: the largest margin of the session is the one that is wrong. Anything that gates on it will gate wrongly.

CAUSE, measured. Angle between the part's long axis and each camera ray (90 = broadside, 0 = end-on):
  fit03   23, 29   min 23
  flip01  26, 26   min 26
  turn90  26, 24   min 24
  turn45   3, 37   min  3     <-- camera A is 3 degrees from looking straight down the part
At 3 degrees that camera sees the part end-on and carries almost no information about along-axis position or which end is which. The fit is effectively single-view for exactly the DOF that decides orientation - and single-view is the configuration already known to fail on this project.

Ruled out: distance from the board. turn45 is the CLOSEST (221mm vs 285/280/303) and the worst, so world-frame extrapolation is not the explanation.

The whole fit degrades together, not just the orientation: seating 38.1mm chosen / 31.3mm alt, against 8.6mm for turn90; containment 45%/71% against 84%/84%. So this is not 'orientation detection is unreliable' in isolation - the registration itself is poor when a camera is end-on, and the orientation error is downstream of that.

FIXES, in order:
1. DETECT AND REFUSE. Compute this angle - it needs only the pose and the board pose, both already to hand - and when the best camera is below ~15 degrees, say the geometry cannot support an orientation call rather than reporting a confident wrong one. Cheap, and it converts a silent failure into an honest one.
2. CELL LAYOUT. Place cameras so no expected part orientation is near end-on to both. With two cameras 52 degrees apart there is a band of part orientations where one is nearly end-on; a third camera on a different bearing removes it.
3. Do NOT gate on the tie-break margin. It is anti-correlated with correctness in this sample.

Supersedes the claim from earlier today that orientation recovery is demonstrated. It is demonstrated for broadside geometry (3 of 3) and fails near end-on (1 of 1).
notes:
REFUTED 2026-09-04 by synthetic sweeps. The original title and diagnosis blamed the part being near end-on to a camera. That was inferred from ONE real failure (turn45, 3 deg off end-on) and it does not survive testing.

TWO SWEEPS, 12 yaw steps each, tone-matched renderer anchored to the rig:
  turn90 rig geometry:  12/12 correct - including at 1.7 and 2.6 deg off end-on,
                        MORE end-on than the real failure that started this.
  turn45 rig geometry:   9/12 correct - flipped at 1, 7 and 22 deg off end-on.
Flips occur at 22 deg (practically broadside) and successes at 2 deg. The end-on angle does not separate the two populations. The proposed refusal gate was aimed at the wrong variable and must NOT be built as specified.

ALSO RULED OUT, same data:
  - rig geometry itself: camera separation 49.8 vs 49.9 deg, board corners and camera distances all near-identical across turn90/turn45/fit03/flip01. The cameras are not the variable.
  - edge pixel count: yaw 105 had 588 edges in camera A and was CORRECT; yaw 0 had 8391 and was FLIPPED.
  - working-area fraction: 0.011 correct, 0.114 flipped. No relationship.

WHAT DOES CORRELATE, with a serious caveat: the tie-break margin. In the turn45-rig sweep, correct trials averaged 21.17 px and flipped ones 2.10 px, and all three flips fell below 4 px. A gate at ~5 px would have caught every synthetic failure at the cost of rejecting two correct answers - an acceptable trade for a refusal gate.

BUT IT WOULD NOT HAVE CAUGHT THE REAL ONE. Real turn45 was wrong with a margin of 16.83 px, the LARGEST of the session. The synthetic run at that same geometry gave 3.53 px. So the harness does not reproduce the real margin behaviour at the single point where both exist, and a margin gate tuned on synthetic data would have passed the one failure we actually observed.

HONEST POSITION: no diagnostic available today predicts an end-for-end failure. The base rate on this part looks like 0-25% depending on placement, consistent with only ~19% of its geometry discriminating the flip. Synthetic cannot settle it alone because it disagrees with the rig precisely where it matters.

NEXT: collect more REAL failures. The cheapest route is a deliberate hunt - shoot 15-20 real captures at varied placements, score each by plate-end projection, and see whether real margins separate. Until then the pipeline should present BOTH hypotheses to the operator rather than pick one, which it already supports (alternatives are in fit.json and the UI has the rotation control).

title: AR fit: residual seating misfit is out-of-plane, not (x,y,yaw)
description:
MEASURED with tools/measure_hull.py (bias-corrected) on fit03:
  centre off  14.3 mm, essentially all along the part's long axis (dx -14.3, dy 0.0)
  axis off     3.3 deg
  worst end   26.8 mm  (~6% of the 432mm part - carries to full size as a fraction)
  containment 72% of visible CAD points land inside the measured silhouette

EVIDENCE THAT (x,y,yaw) IS NOT THE PROBLEM. A silhouette-containment term was added to
the cost (the silhouette is an outer bound, so a CAD point outside it is provably
misplaced) and swept at weight 0/3/10/30/100:
  w=0    14.2 mm / 3.08 deg / 69.6% + 75.0% contained
  w=100  15.4 mm / 2.69 deg / 71.4% + 73.5% contained
and it SATURATES at w>=10 - identical poses to 4 s.f. for 10, 30 and 100. So with the
term fully in charge of the cost, containment still plateaus at ~72%. No (x, y, yaw)
makes this CAD fit that silhouette.

The planar solve holds z and the out-of-plane rotation FIXED (deliberately - six DOF
ran the height to its bound on every run). So the remaining candidates are:
  1. ROLL about the long axis - known to be poorly determined (bd on roll: only 3.4% of
     geometry discriminates, three scoring methods disagree). If the roll is off, the
     projected outline is the wrong SHAPE and no in-plane move fixes it. Most likely.
  2. SEATING HEIGHT - z is fixed at -58mm on the assumption the part rests on the board
     plane with its centre half a height up. If it rests on a different face, or on the
     paper rather than the board, z is wrong.
  3. TILT - the paper is not flat (visible folds in both captures).

NEXT: sweep roll x height, score each by CONTAINMENT rather than by RMS, and see whether
any seating clears ~90%. Containment is the right selector because it is in image space
against a measurement the CAD never touched, and unlike the centroid it carries no bias.

METHOD NOTE, the expensive lesson: the FIRST version of this measurement reported 17.7mm
in the +x direction. The tool's own centroid bias, measured by building a hull from the
CAD's own rendered silhouettes, is 32.3mm in -x - LARGER than the signal and opposite in
sign. Two views bound a shape loosely and the phantom volume is not symmetric. Acting on
the uncorrected number would have pushed the model the wrong way. measure_hull.py now
runs that self-test by default and prints the corrected figure. Any hull-derived
measurement on this rig must be bias-corrected before it means anything.

title: AR fit: edge cost cannot resolve a repetitive truss — pose is ambiguous, not merely hard to find
description:
Measured on the fit03 pair with hidden-line removal working. The two cameras' independent solutions differ by 413.4 mm and 177.2 deg of yaw - an end-for-end flip plus a slide along the part's own length (432 mm). Both look plausible in an overlay.

THE COST CANNOT DISCRIMINATE. Evaluated jointly over visible edges only:
  A-alone solution   22.84 px
  joint fit          23.82 px
  B-alone solution   26.03 px
A ~3 px spread on a ~23 px baseline, between hypotheses 180 deg apart. That is noise. The same blindness shows on other axes: 2.5 px across a 2x change in model SCALE, and 0.6 px across all four ROLL orientations (which face the part rests on).

ROOT CAUSE: the Main Frame is a regular truss. Its bays repeat, so sliding it along its axis by a bay pitch looks nearly identical, and flipping it end-for-end looks nearly identical. Edge matching cannot localise against a periodic structure. This is the SAME result the vault already records for bare sections - 'a steel section's 2D edges do not uniquely determine its pose (parallel/repetitive structure -> many poses align edges well)' - rediscovered on a truss rather than a plain section. It is a property of the information, not of the optimiser.

Multi-view was supposed to break exactly this tie and does not, because each camera falls into a DIFFERENT well and the joint fit averages two incompatible answers.

NOT the cause, all eliminated by measurement: scale (part measures 432 mm, matches the model), world-frame disagreement (board reprojection 0.28/0.32 px, baseline 558.7 vs 561.2 mm), clutter (subject segmentation reduced the search to ~9% of frame), and hidden lines (now removed - 81% of sampled points were far-side edges).

PROPOSED FIX, in order of promise:
1. Use the SEGMENTED SILHOUETTE's extremities. The subject mask already isolates the part; its extent along the axis, back-projected to the board plane, pins the two ends directly. That is a non-periodic constraint and it is nearly free - the segmentation already exists.
2. Weight the asymmetric features. The end plates break the symmetry but contribute a small share of edges; the cost drowns them in repetitive lattice.
3. Enumerate the discrete hypotheses explicitly (yaw, yaw+180, +/- bay pitch) and choose between them on the end-plate region alone rather than on total edge cost.
notes:
RESOLVED 2026-09-04. Confirmed visually by Steve: the chosen orientation is correct.

The edge cost genuinely cannot resolve this - on the final fit the two orientations came out 0.06 px apart, a dead heat. That is not a solver weakness, it is the information: a regular truss matches itself flipped end-for-end.

FIXED by two independent additions, which agree:

1. DISCRIMINATING GEOMETRY (Steve's idea). app/services/model_symmetry.py analyses the CAD alone: apply the candidate symmetry, ask how far each sampled point lands from the nearest original point. Points that map onto themselves carry no orientation information; those that do not are the evidence. Scoring the two hypotheses on those points only (9,522 of 49,642, intersected with visibility) separates them by 15.86 px - primary 13.15 vs flipped 29.01, a 2.2x margin - where all points gave 0.06 px. Wired into the worker as a tie-break that promotes the winner and demotes the loser to a labelled alternative.

2. RENDER-AND-COMPARE (Steve's idea). Rasterise the mesh at the candidate pose and compare against the segmented subject mask. IoU 0.79 for the correct pose vs 0.62 for the flip - ~25% relative separation. Works because the depth-buffer render includes the lattice OPENINGS as holes and the segmentation excludes them too, so internal structure contributes, not just the outline. An earlier test showed only 0.03 separation because it ran at 1/8 resolution, which blurs the openings away.

ALSO USEFUL, from the same symmetry analysis: only 3.4% of points discriminate under a ROLL about the long axis (vs 52% end-for-end). The part is genuinely near-symmetric that way, so roll can never be recovered from edges by any method - it has to come from how the part is seated. Worth knowing before anyone tries.

MEASURED INDEPENDENTLY: a visual-hull plane sweep (no CAD, no fit) put the part's centre at [154, -59] and its axis at 0.4 deg, agreeing with the fit. Aspect ratio 3.62 measured vs 3.73 CAD, within 3% - the print matches the model. Absolute sizes inflate ~20% because a 2-view visual hull over-estimates; that is geometry, not error.
close_reason: Resolved by discriminating-geometry tie-break (2.2x margin) plus render-and-compare (0.79 vs 0.62 IoU); orientation confirmed correct visually.

title: AR fit: no hidden-line removal — projection includes far-side edges
description:
THE remaining blocker on the multi-view fit. We project all 1442 edge polylines (49,642 sampled points) at every pose, including every edge on the FAR side of the object. A camera sees roughly half of them. The rest are phantoms with no counterpart in the image.

CONSEQUENCES, all observed:
- Phantom edges dilute the forward term: they match whatever real edge is nearest, usually belonging to unrelated geometry.
- They make the reverse (bidirectional) term trivially satisfiable, which is why adding it changed nothing - a projection that dense covers everything.
- The cost is therefore nearly blind to pose AND scale: measured only ~2.5px change across a 2x change in model scale.
- A pose displaced along one camera's viewing ray looks right from that camera and wrong from the other. Observed exactly: camera B traces the part closely while camera A is offset and too large, with the world frames verified consistent (board reprojection 0.28/0.32 px, baseline from the pair 558.7mm vs 561.2mm from the calibration set).

FIX: visible-edge extraction, the ViSP/RAPiD approach the vault notes already cite. Rasterise the STL (outputs/ar_models/mainframe_default_1to5.stl, 330KB, already exists) into a z-buffer at the candidate pose; keep only edges not occluded by the mesh. Visibility depends on pose, so it is an outer loop: extract visible edges -> fit -> re-extract -> repeat until stable.

Once this lands, re-enable the bidirectional term (multiview.fit_object_pose reverse_weight, currently default 0.0) - it was reverted because its input was wrong, not because the formulation is.
notes: Everything upstream is verified working: calibration (RMS 0.67/0.64px), rig geometry (baseline 561mm, 52.2deg, 0.97deg spread), board detection 40/40 corners, subject segmentation (~9% of frame, edges only on the part), capture, and the AR Fit UI. This is the only thing between here and a working fit.
close_reason: Hidden-line removal shipped in app/services/visibility.py; 81% of sampled points were far-side edges. Necessary, though not sufficient on its own - see mcp.

title: AR fit: converges to rig structure, not the part
description:
First fits against real photographs (2026-09-04) all converge onto the 2020 extrusion rail instead of the printed part. Two different coarse inits reach an IDENTICAL wrong pose (rvec [0.944, 0.100, -1.002], tvec [695.6, 49.2, 108.2], RMS 31.7px), so it is a deep attractor and not a near miss.

ROOT CAUSE: the model is a long box and the rig's own rails are longer, straighter and higher-contrast than anything on the print. From an edge-matching standpoint the rig looks more like the model than the model does. Camera A yields 8817 edge pixels, only a small fraction of which belong to the part. This matters beyond the bench - the real weld cell will have fixturing and frame members permanently in view.

ALREADY FIXED en route (all committed): degenerate global minimum at 'far away and tiny' (translation bounds + visible_fraction diagnostic); default init assumed the part sits ON the board when it sits beside it (coarse_search over x/y/yaw, distance-transform scored); working-area mask margin so generous it kept 100% of frame; NaN-to-int32 in the mask hull producing a garbage region.

NEXT, in order of expected value:
1. PHYSICAL. Put down the matte mid-grey mat the build spec already calls for - the part currently sits on a textured white desk surrounded by aluminium. And move the part toward the centre of the working area, away from the rails, to get a first successful fit under easy conditions before reintroducing difficulty.
2. Prove the pipeline with a hand-specified init near truth. If it converges and stays, the pipeline is sound and everything remaining is init/clutter. If it still wanders, something deeper is wrong. This is the decisive experiment and has not been run.
3. Tighter coarse grid, refine from the top-N candidates rather than only the best.
4. Consider scoring only edges with orientation consistent with the projected model edge, which would discount a rail running across the part's expected direction.
notes:
RESOLVED 2026-09-04, commit 302330a. Root cause was NOT the rig structure - covering the rails barely moved the answer. Three real causes:

1. PROBLEM FORMULATION (mine). Solving all six DOF when the part rests on the same plane as the board, so its height and tilt are KNOWN. The optimiser used the freedom to buy a lower residual with an unphysical tilt: tvec z pinned at its upper bound on EVERY run, putting the part through the table, rotation reaching ~1.4 rad. fit_object_pose_planar solves only (x, y, yaw). This is also the right formulation for the real cell - a clamped workpiece has known seating.

2. INIT OUT OF GRID RANGE. The coarse grid ran x over -216..576mm while the part sat outside it. No refinement recovers from a grid that does not contain the answer. Now seeded from the edge centroid back-projected onto the plane (estimate_position_from_edges), with the grid centred on that.

3. AUTO CANNY BROKE WHEN THE SCENE GOT CLEANER. Covering the bench in white paper pushed the frame median to ~186, driving median-based thresholds to 124/247 and cutting camera B from 3122 edge pixels to 529 - silhouette only, no internal lattice. At 40/110 it recovers 6936, and the internal lattice is what made the fit possible.

RESULT: RMS 21.4px both views (21.4/21.3 balanced), 100% visible, yaw -88.5 deg. ~9mm on camera B, ~10mm on A at the measured GSD - cm-level, the screening tier ADR 0002 scoped for.

METHOD LESSON: the diagnostic that broke this open was dumping the EDGE PIXELS as an image. Every wrong turn - rails, masks, bounds, thresholds - was visible in one picture of what the solver was actually being fed. Hours were spent reading RMS numbers instead. Make that overlay the first step of any fit investigation, not the last.
close_reason: Fixed: planar formulation + edge-seeded init + corrected Canny thresholds. RMS 21.4px, cm-level, verified visually in both views.

title: classify-frontier reports 'completed' when every chunk failed
description:
A classify-frontier chunk that raises is swallowed by asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) in classify_frontier's run_async. state['done'] is only incremented on success, so the task finishes with status=completed and results={'classified': 0, 'total': N} - and nothing is logged. From the outside it looks like a successful run.

Hit for real on run 761b26b1 (2026-07-17): a 181-ref hollow reclassify returned classified=0 and I only noticed because the sidecar was unchanged. Cause: hollow refs cost ~22s each (measured: 6 refs = 2m13s - long tubes are far slower to raster than bolts), so 181 in one chunk needs ~66 min against _CNC_TIMEOUT=1800s (30 min). asyncio.wait_for killed the subprocess and the exception vanished.

_CLASSIFY_CHUNK=200 is therefore unsafe for any slow part: 200 x 22s = 73 min, well over the timeout. The earlier 2957-ref sweep only survived because it was almost all bolts, which are quick.

Two fixes needed:
1. Never silently succeed. Log each chunk exception and report a failure count in the task result so a caller can tell 'classified 0 of 181' from 'done'.
2. Scale the subprocess timeout with the chunk size rather than using a flat per-chunk budget.
acceptance_criteria: A failing chunk is logged and surfaced in the task result (failed count / error), so a run that classified nothing cannot report plain success; a 200-ref chunk of slow parts completes rather than timing out.
close_reason: b5b: 263 EN 10210 hollow sections added (gen_hollow_sections.py), CSA-primary matching, two library halves mutually exclusive, no NC1 for hollow. On run 761b26b1: 63/64 tubes resolved to real sizes (56x 33.7, 5x 26.9, 2x 114.3x5), 1 bent tube correctly in review, 0 NC1 on hollow. Needed a second fix (415e707): short/raked tubes miss Step 3d's slice (suspect alignment), so _detect_hollow_section now snaps to the library by CSA too. nyt: classify-frontier now logs+returns chunk failures and budgets the timeout per-ref (50b35b2) - found because a 181-ref hollow sweep reported completed having classified 0 (timeout, silently swallowed).

title: Add CHS/SHS/RHS (EN 10210) to the section library with CSA-primary hollow matching
description:
Shape_classifier_info.json holds only OPEN profiles (UB/UC/UBP/RSJ/RSC/PFC/EA/UEA). Hollow sections can only ever be auto-detected by _detect_hollow_section (no designation from a catalogue, no NC1), and since 5wg they are gated out of library matching entirely -> every tube lands at 0.45 review. Run 761b26b1 has 64 of them.

Scope (agreed with Steve 2026-07-17):
1. Populate EN 10210 hot-finished CHS/SHS/RHS (r_o=1.5t, r_i=1.0t). Validated formulae: CHS A=pi*t*(D-t); RHS/SHS A=2t(B+H)-4t^2-1.25*(4-pi)*t^2 (checked: SHS 100x100x5 -> 1873 vs published 1870; SHS 50x50x3 -> 554 vs 554; CHS 168.3x5 -> 2565 vs 2570).
2. CSA-primary matching for hollow only. Evidence: the OBB diameter is unreliable for raked tube - a smooth cylinder has no straight edges for align_by_longest_straight_edge, so the axis skews and the OBB cross-section inflates (measured ODs smear 33.7->41.9 with no clustering on standard sizes). CSA (volume/length) is immune: 63 of 64 land on a real CHS within 8% (33.7x3.0 x30, 33.7x3.2 x26, 33.7x2.6 x3, 114.3x5.0 x2, 26.9x3.2 x2). So score hollow on CSA, with the measured OBB as an UPPER BOUND on the true section (a tube cannot exceed its own bbox) to break CSA ties - 42.4x2.3 and 33.7x3.0 have near-identical CSA (290 vs 289) but a 42.4 cannot fit a 34.9 box.
3. NO NC1 for hollow yet - identify only (designation/CSA/mass), nc1_path stays None as _detect_hollow_section does today. compute_dstv_pose only special-cases U and L, and classify_and_project_holes_dstv projects onto web/flange faces, so tube NC1 would be unvalidated - same risk shape as the EA bug in 5wg. Enabling it is separate work with its own verification.
4. Open shapes must never match a hollow profile and vice versa.

Not doing: EN 10219 cold-formed, EN 10255 pipe (Steve chose 10210 only).
acceptance_criteria: Hollow shapes match only hollow profiles and open shapes only open ones; the 64 CHS in run 761b26b1 resolve to real designations (33.7x3.0/3.2 etc) despite inflated OBB diameters; no NC1 is emitted for any hollow section; genuine UB/PFC/EA matching is unchanged.

On run 761b26b1: 63/64 tubes resolved to real sizes (56x 33.7, 5x 26.9, 2x 114.3x5), 1 bent tube correctly in review, 0 NC1 on hollow. Needed a second fix (415e707): short/raked tubes miss Step 3d's slice (suspect alignment), so _detect_hollow_section now snaps to the library by CSA too. nyt: classify-frontier now logs+returns chunk failures and budgets the timeout per-ref (50b35b2) - found because a 181-ref hollow sweep reported completed having classified 0 (timeout, silently swallowed).

title: BOM item numbers (B001..) are not persisted - any reclassify reshuffles them
description:
assign_bom_items (app/services/bom_manifest.py:132) walks project_state.classifications in INSERTION ORDER and allocates B001.. sequentially. The result is computed fresh on every export and never persisted, so the numbering is only stable while the classification set is unchanged.

Any change to WHICH parts are classified shifts every subsequent B-number, silently breaking matching against a previously issued BOM. This bites immediately on the pending force-reclassify of run 761b26b1: parts dropping below the 0.5 auto-apply threshold (e.g. the 2730 stale 'flanged profile' @0.7 -> 0.45, and handrail tubes 0.90 -> 0.45) leave classifications entirely, so everything after them renumbers.

Note a part changing action (postprocess -> bought-out) does NOT lose its slot, since assign_bom_items counts all of postprocess/bought-out/exclude. Only dropping out of classifications shifts numbering.

Pre-reclass snapshot of run 761b26b1 saved at outputs/bom_snapshots/761b26b1_bom_items_pre-reclass.json (4540 keys -> 358 items, B001-B358).

Fix: persist assignments in the sidecar and reuse them - pin known keys to their existing B-number, allocate only for keys never seen before.
acceptance_criteria: Re-running classification on 761b26b1 leaves every previously-assigned B-number pointing at the same part; new parts get fresh numbers above the existing high-water mark; B155 still resolves to the M20 bolt group.
close_reason: Fixed and verified on run 761b26b1. 5wg: hollowness decided once up front, all library-match paths gated; also fixed _closed_wire_count (4e01709) which had never worked - sliced outside the solid AND called .Length() on a TopoDS_Compound. Handrails now CHS 33.7x3.2, no NC1, review. 0 EA on hollow parts, 0 NC1 on hollow parts. bsk: fastener rule BOUGHT_OUT, bounded by absolute size after bent members (curved UB 8.2M mm3, CHS bend 2.9M mm3) read as bolts - bf752cf. 2513 fasteners; light and heavy now agree 0 disagreements. jcl: pin_bom_items persists assignments; verified 0 of 4141 B-numbers moved across the whole reclassify, B155 still the same 245-off bolt group.

title: Bolts classified SECTION - bolt head reads as a flange (rule 8)
description:
M20-class bolts classify as SECTION because part_classifier rule 8 reads the bolt HEAD as a flange: thk_max (head, 20.09) / t_eff (shank, ~8.3) = 2.41 >= SECTION_THK_RATIO (1.5) -> 'flanged, no library match'.

Evidence (run 761b26b1): 0:1:1:2792 L=68 head 37x37 shank dia 19.56 (CSA 312 ~ M20's 314) i21=1.0 (axisymmetric solid of revolution) n_holes=0 bends=0 elongation=1.84 vol=39368. Also 0:1:1:3221 (L=55, M16-class) and 0:1:1:1215 (L=73).

These are BOM items B155 (qty 245!), B156 (qty 4), B157 (qty 13) - all currently auto-classified 'postprocess' (CNC).

catalogue_products.match_catalogue_product is NAME-based and this model is 100% unnamed (every node 'Unnamed_*'), so it cannot catch them. Needs a geometric rule.

Proposed signature (verified against all three): axisymmetric (inertia_ratio_21 ~ 1.0) AND solid (n_holes == 0) AND stubby (elongation <= ~8) AND has a head (thk_max_over_teff >= 1.5) -> BOUGHT_OUT. Must sit AFTER rule 4 so hollow round tubes (handrail, also i21=1.0) are unaffected; a plain round bar (no head, thk ratio ~1) is unaffected.
acceptance_criteria: 0:1:1:2792/3221/1215 classify BOUGHT_OUT; handrail tubes (hollow, i21~1.0) unaffected; round bar without a head unaffected; no regression on eval_rules.py.

Handrails now CHS 33.7x3.2, no NC1, review. 0 EA on hollow parts, 0 NC1 on hollow parts. bsk: fastener rule BOUGHT_OUT, bounded by absolute size after bent members (curved UB 8.2M mm3, CHS bend 2.9M mm3) read as bolts - bf752cf. 2513 fasteners; light and heavy now agree 0 disagreements. jcl: pin_bom_items persists assignments; verified 0 of 4141 B-numbers moved across the whole reclassify, B155 still the same 245-off bolt group.

title: Parallel background classification for large flat models
description: Per-request classify is too slow for flat models with thousands of parts (761b26b1: 117MB, 61s file-open, 3.24s/part -> ~4.3h single-threaded; batching re-opened the file per batch and hit 30-min timeouts). New POST /cnc-analysis/classify-frontier runs a single background task that fans chunks (200) across cores (cpu-1 concurrency, one core left for uvicorn), persists to the sidecar as chunks complete (serialised by an asyncio.Lock), and reports progress via GET .../classify-frontier/status. GET /cnc-analysis/classification returns the cached map for progressive merging. Frontend _classifyFrontier now starts/reconnects to the task and polls, applying results progressively; survives navigation (server-side task) and resumes on re-open (already-classified refs skipped). Verified: task persists results; 3 concurrent workers confirmed via ps.
close_reason: Implemented + verified. Backend classify-frontier background task (parallel across cpu-1 cores, incremental sidecar persist, progress, idempotent/reconnect) + classification read endpoint; frontend _classifyFrontier starts/polls the task, applies progressively, survives navigation, auto-continues on progress. Verified end-to-end: 6-ref task completed + persisted; 3 concurrent workers confirmed.

title: Flat files with thousands of parts: classify/CNC workers hit ARG_MAX; frontier not batched
description: A flat STEP file with thousands of top-level parts (run 761b26b1: 4731 single-solid + 153 multi-solid, no assemblies) failed auto-classify with 500 '[Errno 7] Argument list too long'. The classify worker (and the CNC analysis worker) passed ref_ids/member_ids/parent_names/instance_counts as command-line arguments, overflowing ARG_MAX. Also _classifyFrontier sent all refs in one request (blocking minutes, all-or-nothing). Fix: pass the large JSON payloads to both workers via stdin; batch _classifyFrontier (250/req) with incremental auto-classify so results stream in. Verified classify on 761b26b1 refs post-fix (single + multi-solid).
close_reason: Classify + CNC analysis workers now receive ref_ids/member_ids/parent_names/instance_counts via stdin (was argv -> ARG_MAX on thousands of parts). _classifyFrontier batches at 250/request with incremental auto-classify. Verified classify on 761b26b1 (single + multi-solid) returns results; all workers compile.

title: BOM Refined '—': cached-CNC-result load wholesale-replaces _cncAnalysisResults, wiping refined cache
description: After analysis open loads the refined-class cache into _cncAnalysisResults (46 entries incl 0:1:1:33=FORMED_PLATE), the best-effort getCncResult() load did _cncAnalysisResults = resp.results — a wholesale replace. title: Standard BOM not refreshed after classifying from the tree
description: Classifying a part via the tree CNC/BO/EXC buttons (_classifyNode/_unclassifyNode/_applyClassification) called _refreshNativeBomIfOpen, which only re-rendered the Full BOM (#native-bom-panel) — the Standard BOM (#parts-list-panel) was left stale. title: Display parent assembly name for generic-named leaf parts (SOLID/COMPOUND)
description: STEP exporters wrap single-part assemblies as 'AssemblyName -> {SOLID (real geometry), COMPOUND (empty artifact)}'. The pipeline keeps the SOLID and auto-excludes the empty COMPOUND (correct), but labels the BOM/tree row with the generic leaf name 'SOLID', while the recognisable name ('Column Plate CP1') sits on the parent assembly. Result: BOM/auto-detected items don't match the tree and reconciliation is impossible; excluded COMPOUND siblings look like the part was dropped. Fix: when a leaf's name is generic (SOLID/COMPOUND/blank) AND it has solid geometry, display the parent assembly name (already captured in cnc_parent_names). Apply only to kept (solid-bearing) nodes so the excluded empty COMPOUND keeps its generic name + EXC badge, disambiguating the pair. Touches: frontend tree render + BOM walk, bom_builder (Full BOM mark), bom_excel (_build_bom_data name), bom_manifest (member_name). Display-only; no geometry/classification change. Run c25bf2c8.
close_reason: Implemented resolve_display_name parent-name fallback across bom_builder, bom_excel, and frontend (tree + Full BOM + CSV). Solid-bearing generic leaves show parent assembly name; no-solid artifacts keep generic name + EXC. Verified on c25bf2c8. Tests in tests/test_bom_builder.py.

title: AR: move test target from single element to a welded assembly
description: Single bare section is unrealistic AND the hardest pose case: near-symmetric/repetitive edges (ambiguous correspondence + markerless divergence), small faces (tiny/occluded markers, often only 1 visible = weak tilt/depth pose), and no welds to ratify (the tool's actual purpose). A real welded assembly is easier: distinctive multi-plane geometry, room for 3-4 large well-separated markers (constellation + fused solve want this), more co-visible tags, and real welds to validate. Next test: pick an assembly with existing CAD + connection/weld data (known run_id), place 3-4 spread markers, shoot several 3/4 oblique views (>=2 markers each), calibrate constellation from close-ups, anchor once from a clean wide solve, auto-align the obliques. Validates the product as intended rather than stress-testing the weakest config.

title: AR auto-align: reject outlier markers + report per-marker residuals
description: Auto-align fuses every visible registered marker equally into one solvePnP. A single badly-registered tag (e.g. constellation markers 2/3 with residual chain error) drags the whole pose, so alignment varies a lot by which markers are in frame (held-out: 8448=5px, 8446=8px, but 8450=45px using markers 1+2+3). Fix: after the fused solve, compute each marker's individual reprojection residual; if the worst is a clear outlier (> abs threshold AND >> median of the rest), drop it and re-solve. Return per-marker residuals + dropped IDs and surface in UI. Keeps >=1 marker.

title: BOM export floods 'Unknown Items' with solid-level classification keys (multi-solid parts)
description: Server-side BOM builders (bom_excel._build_bom_data, bom_manifest.assign_bom_items / build_manifest_rows) resolve classification node_id->ref_id via _build_node_to_ref, which only maps tree leaf instance ids. Multi-solid parts classified per-solid are stored under '<ref>:s<n>' keys (frontend keys solid children by prototype ref_id). These keys aren't in node_to_ref, so each falls back to itself as a bogus ref, finds no member name and no CNC result, and lands in the Excel 'Unknown Items' sheet. Frontend _resolveClassification handles this (strips :s<n>, remaps) so the UI is correct; only the export is wrong. Repro run e8a0ba3c: 55 solid keys across 3 multi-solid parts (Main Frame, Top Support, Reinforcement) show as 55 garbage Unknown rows instead of 3 CNC items. Fix: add shared resolver that strips ':s<n>' suffix before node_to_ref lookup, used by all server BOM builders.

Reuse the cross-section raster (already computed for holes) to derive H/W/area for the library match instead of re-slicing. Then: worker + endpoint, sidecar storage (separate 'classification' key), frontend triggers it on explode and feeds _autoClassifyFromRefinedResults. title: Synthetic data: keep as regenerable manifests, and plan the learned/geometric split
description:
Steve's point: we will end up with an AI / programmed-geometry hybrid, so keep what we generate.

WHAT TO KEEP, AND WHAT NOT TO.
Renders are a deterministic function of (mesh, pose, rig, renderer params, seed) and cost minutes to reproduce - the survey's 120 images are 216MB. Store MANIFESTS and regenerate. synth_capture.py now records every one of those fields plus the code version in truth.json, so a sample can be rebuilt byte-for-byte.

What is genuinely irreplaceable is the other half:
  - the five REAL capture sets with verified poses. Only these can tell us the synthetic
    is lying, and they cost bench time to make.
  - the LABELS tied to conditions (correct / flipped / fit-failed, with end-on angle,
    edge count, margin, seating error).
  - the FAILURES above all. Real turn45 - wrong with the largest margin of the session -
    is worth more than a thousand synthetic successes, because it is the one place where
    synthetic and real demonstrably disagree.

THE TRAP TO AVOID: mixing renderer generations under one label. The pre-shadow, pre-tone renderer modelled a different world (seating 2.5mm against the rig's 8.6mm). A model trained across both would be learning two domains averaged together. Hence code_commit and the full renderer block in every manifest.

DOMAIN RANDOMISATION IS ALREADY AVAILABLE. paper, ink, ambient, diffuse, sun, shadow, soft, noise, blur and seed are all parameters. Varying them per sample is exactly what a sim-to-real training set wants - the model then cannot latch onto our particular lighting. Today they are fixed to match the rig, which is right for MEASUREMENT and wrong for training; both modes are wanted.

WHERE A LEARNED COMPONENT BELONGS, on this project's own evidence:
  - COARSE POSE PROPOSAL. Currently a grid search that has repeatedly failed to contain
    the answer. Learned pose regression / render-and-compare (MegaPose, CosyPose) is
    mature and this is its natural job.
  - ORIENTATION DISAMBIGUATION. The exact thing our geometric tie-break gets wrong, and
    where no hand-built diagnostic has separated the populations - end-on angle, edge
    count, working area and two symmetry metrics have all been tried and refuted.
  - SCREENING. Which parts are feasible at all. Edge count is the first thing that
    separated the survey data; a learned screen could do better with the same labels.

WHERE IT DOES NOT: refinement and verification stay geometric. The geometric path gives mm-level accuracy and, more importantly, is AUDITABLE - measure_hull.py scores a pose against a measurement the CAD never touched, and mark_ends.py puts the claim on the photograph where a person can check it. This project's recurring failure is confident-and-wrong, and a network's confidence cannot be audited the way a residual can.

SO THE SPLIT IS: learned components PROPOSE, geometric components VERIFY AND REFINE. Never the reverse. Every learned output should be checkable by something that does not share its assumptions.

title: Rig: raise exposure ~20% — paper reads 196, headroom to 255
description:
Steve's observation: the synthetic renders looked clearer and brighter than the rig, and the better fix is to brighten the rig rather than dim the render.

MEASURED off turn90 (camera B68DE55F, greyscale):
  real rig     mean 155.7  median 182  p10 57  p90 196  contrast 139
  synthetic    mean 201.3  median 237  p10 28  p90 239  contrast 211

Paper reads p90=196, so there is headroom to 255 and nothing is clipping. Raising exposure ~20% would put paper near 235 without blowing highlights, and a brighter image with a wider absolute gap between part and paper is easier for Otsu to split - which is the step that segments the subject and therefore governs how much of the part the fit ever sees.

CALIBRATION SURVIVES THIS. Exposure does not affect intrinsics; focus and zoom do. So the existing profile stays valid PROVIDED focus remains locked at its current value. Re-lock with tools/webcam_capture.py lock after changing, and confirm focus_absolute is unchanged before and after - if focus moves, the calibration must be redone.

WHAT WILL NEED RE-CHECKING: the Canny thresholds. They are fixed absolute numbers (40/110) precisely because auto-thresholding broke when the scene got cleaner - see bead vh4, where an A0 sheet pushed the frame median to ~186 and camera B collapsed from 3122 edge pixels to 529. Raising exposure moves the histogram the same way. So after any exposure change, re-shoot one capture and check edge_pixels per view in the fit diagnostics before trusting a result.

ALSO UPDATE THE RENDERER. tools/synth_capture.py now defaults to --paper 196 --ink 55, matched to the CURRENT rig. If the rig is brightened, re-measure and raise those defaults to match, or the harness will be modelling a rig that no longer exists.

Blocked while the rig is offline (network reboot).

title: AR fit: roll (seating) is not recoverable from two views — operator supplies it
description:
MEASURED, not assumed. On the 1:5 Main Frame, roll about the part's long axis cannot be determined from the current two-camera setup:

- Only 3.4% of sampled geometry discriminates under a 180 deg roll, against 52% end-for-end.
- The three available scores DISAGREE about it: full edge cost prefers 180 by 1.13px (correct), discriminating-points prefers 0 by 0.44px (wrong), render-and-compare is tied at 0.002 (no signal).
- The method that decisively settled the end-for-end flip (2.2x margin) gets roll backwards.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT (Steve's domain knowledge): the hole pattern. The CAD has 172 circular edges and ALL 172 move under a 180 deg roll - median 16.1mm, max 35.2mm. That is 100% discriminating where the structure is 3.4%. But at 1:5 the holes are 1.4-5.6mm, which at the measured GSD (0.42-0.49 mm/px) is 3-12 pixels. Hough found 2 circles inside the part on camera A and 0 on camera B. Correct in principle, unresolvable at this resolution.

RESOLUTION REQUIRED, as a spec input for the cell:
  coarse pose            ~0.45 mm/px   (have it)
  read a 5.6mm hole      ~0.28 mm/px   (~1.7x better - a 4K Brio gets there, ~0.21)
  read a 1.4mm hole      ~0.07 mm/px   (~6x - needs the close camera)
This is direct evidence for the two-tier camera design already in the vault: wide pair for registration, close camera for feature reading.

CURRENT ANSWER: the operator supplies the seating. The AR Fit tab has rotation buttons (X90 / Y90 / Y180 / Z90) that apply the rotation about the part's own centre and RE-SOLVE position and yaw around it - seconds, no coarse search. Endpoint POST /api/v1/ar-fit/adjust; worker flags --from-fit and --rotate. In production the fixture fixes seating anyway, and the control remains useful as an override.

OBSERVED, worth following up: imposing the correct roll improved RMS 26.29 -> 22.40, a 15% gain, well clear of the 0.06px that separated the end-for-end hypotheses. So the cost CAN see the difference once a seating is imposed and refitted around, even though it cannot find it by search. If that holds across several captures with the part deliberately placed different ways up, the pipeline could try each roll, refit, and rank - showing the margin as it now does for the flip. One 15% result on one pair is not enough to automate on.

title: AR fit: Canny thresholds need setting by hand on a clean background
description:
auto_canny_thresholds() takes the median of the frame (or of the kept region) and derives low/high from it. That assumes a scene with a normal tonal spread. On the test cell - a mid-grey part on a white A0 sheet - the median is ~186, giving thresholds 124/247, which catch only the part's outer silhouette. Camera B produced 529 edge pixels instead of 3122, losing the entire internal lattice, and the fit cannot succeed on a silhouette alone.

Currently worked around by passing --canny-low 40 --canny-high 110 explicitly, which yields 6936.

The in-mask median does not help (186 vs 187) because the working area is also mostly white. Needs a statistic that reflects the SUBJECT rather than the background: candidates are Otsu on the kept region, a percentile of the gradient magnitude rather than of intensity, or targeting a desired edge-pixel count by bisection. The last is crude but directly expresses what we actually want.
notes: Bit us on 2026-09-04: making the scene cleaner (which was the right physical move) silently starved the edge detector. Any auto-threshold on a deliberately uniform background is suspect.

title: AR: image edge extraction (Canny -> edge_pixels) + headless multi-view fit driver
description: THE missing link between the working solver and real photos. fit_object_pose() in app/services/multiview.py takes edge_pixels as an INPUT; the 4-view 0.00-0.05deg result was on SYNTHETIC points. Nothing in the repo turns a JPEG into those pixels - grep for Canny/edge_pixels finds only the multiview consumer. Build: (1) image -> edge pixels (Canny + tuning for oxidised/matte-print steel, undistort-aware); (2) per-photo camera pose from the ChArUco board in shot via board_pose.charuco_board_pose; (3) drive fit_object_pose against outputs/ar_models/mainframe_default_1to5.json; (4) overlay PNG of projected CAD edges vs image. Headless CLI first (folder of photos + calibration profile in, pose + overlay out) so it can be built and synthetic-tested BEFORE the Pi arrives, then pointed at real captures. De-risks cg0 without needing the UI. CAMERA-AGNOSTIC - not blocked on the Pi.
notes:
DONE 2026-09-02. Built and verified end-to-end on synthetic imagery.

SHIPPED:
- app/services/charuco.py - board construction/detection EXTRACTED from routers/calibration.py (which now delegates). One definition, because a divergent copy fails silently with zero corners.
- app/services/image_edges.py - Canny edge pixels + board masking.
- app/services/multiview_fit.py - profile/model load, per-view build, overlay render, orchestration. In app/ not tools/ so the cg0 endpoint can reuse it.
- tools/fit_multiview.py - headless CLI. docker-compose.yml now bind-mounts ./tools (was neither COPYed nor mounted).
- tools/webcam_capture.py - USB webcam capture for a non-Pi host.
- tests/test_image_edges.py (10) + tests/test_multiview_fit.py (7). Full suite 105 passed, 1 pre-existing failure (tlz, known stale test).

THREE FINDINGS worth keeping:
1. BOARD FRAME Z POINTS AWAY FROM THE CAMERA. A camera decoding an OpenCV ChArUco board solves to a centre at NEGATIVE board Z. So resting on the board = object at negative Z. default_init_pose was placing it at +Z, i.e. under the table. Now measured from the solved poses via camera_side_of_board(); test_board_is_legible_from_negative_z locks it.
2. MASKING THE LATTICE IS NOT ENOUGH. The ArUco bit patterns inside the white squares are the bulk of the board edges - lattice-only masking left ~58% of them (19189 -> 11154) and the fit latched on. Filling marker quads from board.getObjPoints() takes board-only edges to ZERO while covering only ~7% of frame.
3. A GOOD RMS AT A WRONG POSE IS A WRONG POSE - reproduced. One view scored RMS 11.97 vs two views 10.98, yet was 8x worse in translation (17.07mm vs 2.07mm). Same failure that sank the single-image markerless spikes.

ACCURACY (synthetic, 2 views): 11.64 deg cold init -> 1.85 deg / 2.23 mm. Residual dominated by the test's crude 2px wireframe render (Canny sees both sides of each drawn line) plus ~50% of object edge pixels lost to the board mask - NOT a solver limit.

KNOWN LIMITATION: the board mask also erases object edges wherever the part overlaps board pattern. In the real cell put the part on the matte mat, not on the board.

NOT YET DONE: never run on a real photograph. Needs the rig + real intrinsics.

title: Plates show as 'Unknown Items' in BOM when no DXF has been generated
description:
The Excel BOM 'Unknown Items' sheet is populated by postprocess parts whose HEAVY cnc result type is None/unknown — i.e. it buckets on 'has a DXF/NC1 been generated', not on the part's identity. So a part correctly light-identified as PLATE @0.90 shows as 'unknown' purely because heavy CNC analysis (which generates the DXF and stamps type='plate') hasn't run on it.

Observed on run 761b26b1 (C24025-Model, 2026-07-18): of 1782 postprocess parts only 196 had a heavy CNC result; 1586 had none, of which **1337 are light-identified PLATE** and 249 SECTION. All 1337 plates appear under 'Unknown Items' despite being correctly identified.

Root cause is the light/heavy classification split: the light pass knows it's a plate, but the BOM presentation trusts only the heavy result. This is the identify-vs-produce conflation from the v3 review — a part IS a plate before any DXF is cut.

2.0 workaround: run heavy CNC analysis over the remaining postprocess plates to generate their DXFs; they then move from 'Unknown Items' to 'CNC Items'.

Proper fix (v3): BOM views project over Identity (+ Decision), with a separate output_status (pending/generated/verified). 'No artifact yet' must never render as 'unknown'. See PSS-Vault/projects/cad-automation/decisions/2026-07-18-v3-spec.md section 6, and the classification-bolts-and-hollow-sections note follow-ups.
acceptance_criteria: A part identified as PLATE (or any class) shows under its class in the BOM regardless of whether its DXF/NC1 has been generated; a separate status distinguishes 'output pending' from 'generated'. 'Unknown Items' contains only genuinely unidentified parts.

title: Unmatched 'flanged profile' heuristic auto-classifies non-standard parts (handrails) as CNC section
description: On handrail-heavy models the classifier calls thousands of parts SECTION via the 'flanged profile' heuristic (part_classifier rule 8, conf 0.70) — which fires only when the library did NOT match, i.e. the OBB/cross-section doesn't correspond to an available standard profile. At 0.70 (>0.5) these auto-commit to CNC, but many are handrail standards (bought-out). Geometry can't tell procured from fabricated. Fix: lower the unmatched 'flanged' heuristic to 0.45 (below the auto-apply threshold) so it surfaces as review with a SECTION suggestion instead of auto-CNC; genuine library matches (0.85) still auto-classify. Added force option to classify-frontier to re-classify after the rule change. Verified: force re-classify returns SECTION 0.45 'flanged, no library match'.
close_reason: Fixed: part_classifier rule 8 now 0.45 (review) for unmatched flanged sections; classify-frontier gains force=true. Verified on 761b26b1 refs -> SECTION 0.45 'flanged, no library match'.

title: Lazy detection: don't analyse a multi-solid's solids until it's exploded
description: On load, _classifyFrontier/_collectFrontierRefs eagerly classifies unexploded top-level multi-solids. Classifying a multi-solid analyses ALL its solids, which for a large part (e.g. 400 solids ~80s) can exceed the CNC timeout and kill the subprocess. Change: skip unexploded multi-solids in _collectFrontierRefs (detect on explode instead); an exploded multi-solid is added for per-solid detection. Moves the analysis cost from load-time to explode-time; the tree is usable immediately. Weldments won't auto-classify until exploded (consistent with skip-until-exploded).

title: Single-multi-solid files: BOM/NC-Index/DXF exports collapsed to one item
description: A STEP file that is a single part_multi_solid of N discrete parts (flat export, e.g. run 1f047f40 with 400 solids) collapsed to ONE line in the server-side XLSX BOM, and the NC Index + DXF/NC1 zips listed every solid/placement including excluded ones. Root cause: the backend BOM pipeline (assign_bom_items / build_manifest_rows / _build_bom_data) deliberately collapses a multi-solid's sub-solids onto the parent ref (weldment model), and the DXF/NC1 zip had no intra-solid dedup or per-solid CNC filter. Fix: when a multi-solid's solids are classified individually, emit one BOM Item per unique solid (deduped by intra_solid_groups, CNC/postprocess-filtered), keyed by solid key, shared across BOM sheet + NC Index + DXF zip. Weldments (parent-ref classified) still collapse. Verified on 1f047f40: BOM 116 rows, NC Index 72, DXF 38 / NC1 34.

Verified on 1f047f40: BOM 116 rows, NC Index 72, DXF 38 / NC1 34, IDs consistent.

title: Fresh multi-solid explode doesn't auto-classify solids or populate BOM (self-heals only after save+reopen)
description:
Repro: run 12b7a61e (a single part_multi_solid 'Product' with 400 solids, no assembly). On first explode, the 400 solids are NOT auto-classified and the BOM shows only the combined item. After a save+reopen it works.

Root cause: _explodeMultiSolid/_pollSolidsTask add generated solid children only to _solidChildrenCache + the DOM, never to this._treeData. _autoClassifyFromRefinedResults walks this._treeData and only descends into an exploded part_multi_solid when node.children exists (it doesn't on a fresh explode), so per-solid refined_class is never applied. The explode-time _classifyFrontier() also runs BEFORE the async solids arrive, and nothing re-runs auto-classify/BOM render after _pollSolidsTask completes.

Why reopen self-heals: on save, backend _embed_solid_children (analysis.py) writes the solids into the sidecar assembly_tree; on next open this._treeData has children, so auto-classify descends and classifies (398/400 solids are confident in this file).

Fix: when solids arrive (in _pollSolidsTask completion + the cached-children branch of _explodeMultiSolid), embed them into matching this._treeData nodes using the same shape as backend _embed_solid_children, then re-run _autoClassifyFromRefinedResults(), apply the resulting classifications to the new solid DOM <li>s, and re-render the parts list/BOM. Makes fresh-explode identical to reopen.
close_reason: Fixed: fresh multi-solid explode now embeds solids into _treeData, auto-classifies from per-solid refined_class, and paints the tree DOM immediately (previously classifications applied to state/BOM but not the tree rows, appearing only after a second reload). Validated end-to-end on run 1f047f40: 400/400 solids classified (368 CNC + 32 exclude), consolidated to 110 unique, CNC analysis produced 249 DXF + 83 NC1, 0 errors.

title: AR ratification: per-part RAG screening report (as-built vs as-designed)
description: Screening/triage, NOT metrology (ADR 0002). After registering assembly pose on a TRUSTED BACKBONE (main frame/fixture/known-good datum), test each CAD part as a hypothesis (present vs absent vs flipped/mirrored vs wrong-item vs displaced) by projecting its edges into the calibrated views and scoring agreement. Output a RAG report per part (and per weld): OK / CHECK (occluded/ambiguous) / MISSING / BACKWARDS / WRONG-ITEM / DISPLACED. Rides on large cm-level signals so coarse pose suffices. 'Not detected' must be CHECK(occluded) not false MISSING -> 4-camera coverage. Reuse _is_mirrored/chiral_key for 'installed backwards', ref_id for part identity, weld paths for weld checks. Roadmap Phase 3.

title: AR: multi-image manual correspondences (two-view bundle solve)
description: Let the user click correspondences across TWO photos (e.g. close-ups of each end of a section) and combine into one pose for the whole section. Today each solve uses correspondences from one photo against one camera pose. Two photos are two camera poses, so points cannot be pooled into a single solvePnP. Fix: solve each photo for its own camera pose against the shared CAD vertices, then jointly bundle-adjust (reuse least_squares/Huber from constellation.py) with the CAD as the rigid link. Well-spread points on both ends pin the section far tighter than 4 cramped points on one end (the wobble seen with the loupe). Alternative already-working path: a marker visible in both ends via the constellation. This bead is the pure-markerless multi-image path.

title: AR marker-SLAM constellation calibration
description: Resolve the wide-vs-close tension on long parts: close shots show 2+ markers but not enough section to click; wide shots show the section but only 1 marker. Build a marker pose-graph: detect markers across many photos, chain co-visible markers' relative poses into one constellation frame (no CAD needed), then one manual solve on a wide shot anchors the whole constellation to the model -> per-marker T(marker->model) for ALL markers -> existing auto-solve fuses any visible subset. Endpoints: /ar/calibrate-constellation (multi-photo), /ar/anchor-constellation (one solved photo). Reuses ar_markers + auto-solve.
notes: FIXED via bundle adjustment + validated on real data (iphone/const). Global RMS 61.8->14.3px; broken 2&3 long-hop links 212->5.2px, 93->6.1px on held-out photos; good links unchanged. BA = joint optimise all marker+camera poses over all corner observations, Huber loss, scipy least_squares, init from spanning tree. Implemented in constellation.bundle_adjust + wired into calibrate-constellation (returns rms_before/after). 41 tests pass. FOLLOW-UPS: (1) one photo (8450, [1,2,3]) still 45px - likely noisy/oblique detection in that shot; (2) surface auto-solve reproj_rms in the UI as a per-photo quality flag (warn when high) - cheap soundness win; (3) marker_size assumed uniform (100mm) - verify against real measured size for metric scale.

title: Known catalogue-product BO detection (Unistrut, etc.)
description: Some bought-out items ARE confidently identifiable (unlike the general make/buy call). Unistrut = proprietary strut-channel (channel w/ inturned rolled lips), always BO, identifiable by name ('SUPP UNIST...') and by its distinctive cross-section. Build a small extensible 'known catalogue products' list mapping name/shape -> BOUGHT_OUT. CAVEAT: name match must be specific -- 'SUPP UNIST PLATE 2mm' is a CNC plate, not strut (rule: contains 'unist' AND NOT 'plate'). Start with name rules; add the rolled-lip channel shape detector for unnamed cases. Only 6 parts/3 names in current corpus but the pattern generalises.
notes:
REOPENED: name-based rule alone is insufficient — part name is NOT guaranteed
(Steve, 2026-06-09). Name rule (catalogue_products.py) stays as a high-confidence
shortcut, but need SHAPE-based Unistrut detection for unnamed parts:
signature = thin uniform wall (low t_eff) + open channel envelope (~41mm squarish)
+ inturned ROLLED LIPS (convex bends near the opening -> n_convex_bends>0) making
the section nearly-closed (slot, not full hole). Approach: cross-section template
/ signature match on the raster + bend faces. Until then Unistrut without the name
falls through to the geometric tree (likely mislabelled formed/section).

Signature: constant tube profile but curved/multi-bend centreline -> centreline_length (=volume/CSA) >> dim_long; slice perpendicular to bbox-long-axis is not a clean constant profile. Added 'Bent section' to the labelling gallery (collate_candidates.py).
